stem: Why did Chicago become the center of the American cattle trade after the long drives began?

stimulus.source_note: Joseph G. McCoy, Historic Sketches of the Cattle Trade of the West and Southwest (1874), ch. 2. Public domain. Text verified against the 1874 edition as quoted in the Stanford-adjacent SVHS lesson (svhs.co/lesson/d1-5-9-12/) and the SweetStudy transcription of the same chapter.
stimulus.text:
Joseph G. McCoy, Historic Sketches of the Cattle Trade of the West and Southwest (1874), Chapter 2:

"Many ranchmen entirely neglected their stock, for they were regarded as not worth caring for. Stocks of cattle were, in certain sections, offered at prices ranging from one to two dollars per head, and that often without finding a purchaser. ... a select, matured animal, worth five or six dollars in Texas — was worth in the Northern markets more than ten times that amount."

"We have heard the number of cattle that had crossed Red river during 1866 put down as high as 260,000 head."

"Twenty-five to thirty-five days is the usual time required to bring a drove from Red river to the southern line of Kansas, a distance of between two hundred and fifty and three hundred miles..."

options.text: Chicago was the only city where cattle could legally be sold
options.misconception: Background: cattle were bought and sold at many railheads, including Abilene and Kansas City; no law confined the trade to Chicago.

options.text: Chicago sat on the Pacific coast, closest to the Texas herds
options.misconception: Background: Chicago sits on Lake Michigan in Illinois, far from the Pacific and far from Texas.

options.text: Railroads brought cattle to Chicago, and refrigerated cars carried beef east
Chicago's city government paid ranchers to drive their herds there
options.misconception: Background: no city paid ranchers to come; the trade followed the railroads and the packing houses, not a subsidy.

rationales.A: Background: Abilene, Kansas City, and other rail towns all traded cattle. Background: Chicago won the trade by scale, not by law.
rationales.B: Background: Chicago is a Great Lakes city in Illinois. The Pacific coast is two thousand miles away.
rationales.C: Background from the books: the drives ended at Kansas railheads, the trains carried the cattle to Chicago's packing houses, and newly invented refrigerated rail cars carried dressed beef on to eastern cities.
rationales.D: Background: the packers came to Chicago for the rails and the labor, not for a city payment. No such payment existed.
rationales.general:
Think of Chicago as the funnel: everything poured in, and beef poured out.
1. Follow the cattle: they walked to the Kansas railheads, where the railroad took over.
2. Follow the beef. Background: Chicago slaughtered and packed it, and refrigerated cars kept it fresh on the trip east.
3. Name the chain. Trail, rail, packing house, refrigerated car: each link made the next one pay.
Remember: a city becomes a center when it sits where the most links meet.
